facts.statement: The shark grew up to 8 meters long and weighed approximately 5000 kilograms.
facts.quote: Measuring up to 8 m in length and weighing around 5000 kg, Cretoxyrhina was one of the largest sharks of its time.

facts.statement: Its teeth were up to 8 centimeters long, razor-like, and had thick enamel designed for stabbing and slicing.
facts.quote: Its teeth, up to 8 cm long, were razor-like and had thick enamel built for stabbing and slicing prey.

facts.statement: Hydrodynamic calculations suggest the shark could reach burst speeds of up to 70 kilometers per hour.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina was also among the fastest-swimming sharks, with hydrodynamic calculations suggesting burst speeds of up to 70 km/h.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that the shark hunted by lunging at high speeds to inflict powerful blows, relying on strong eyesight.
facts.quote: It has been speculated that Cretoxyrhina hunted by lunging at its prey at high speeds to inflict powerful blows, similar to the great white shark today, and relied on strong eyesight to do so.

facts.statement: Analysis of vertebrae indicates the shark reached sexual maturity at four to five years and had a lifespan of nearly forty years.
facts.quote: Studies have successfully calculated its life history using vertebrae from some of the skeletons. Cretoxyrhina grew rapidly during early ages and reached sexual maturity at around four to five years of age. Its lifespan has been calculated to extend to nearly forty years.

facts.statement: Anatomical analysis suggests the shark used regional endothermy and had facial features similar to thresher and crocodile sharks.
facts.quote: Anatomical analysis of the Cretoxyrhina skeletons revealed that the shark possessed facial and optical features most similar to that in thresher sharks and crocodile sharks and had a hydrodynamic build that suggested the use of regional endothermy.

facts.statement: The shark preferred subtropical to temperate pelagic waters but may have lived in water as cold as 5 degrees Celsius.
facts.quote: It preferred mainly subtropical to temperate pelagic environments but may have occurred in waters as cold as 5 C.

facts.statement: Louis Agassiz reclassified the teeth as a single species in 1843, noting their similarity to species in the now-invalid genus Oxyrhina.
facts.quote: In the third volume of his book Recherches sur les poissons fossiles, published in 1843, Swiss naturalist Louis Agassiz reexamined Mantell's eight teeth. Using them and another tooth from the collection of the Strasbourg Museum (whose exact location was unspecified but also came from England), he concluded that the fossils actually pertained to a single species of extinct shark that held strong dental similarities with the three species then classified in the now-invalid genus Oxyrhina, O. hastalis, O. xiphodon, and O. desorii.

facts.statement: Charles H. Sternberg discovered the first skeleton in 1890 and described it in a 1907 paper.
facts.quote: Charles H. Sternberg discovered the first skeleton in 1890, which he described in a 1907 paper:

facts.statement: The genus is traditionally placed in the family Cretoxyrhinidae, though some researchers propose it belongs in Alopiidae or Lamnidae.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina is traditionally classified as the likely sole member of the family Cretoxyrhinidae but other taxonomic placements have been proposed, such as within the Alopiidae and Lamnidae.

facts.statement: It is debated whether competition with the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus contributed to the shark's extinction.
facts.quote: One factor in this demise may have been increasing pressure from competition with predators that arose around the same time, most notably the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: Charles R. Eastman published an analysis of a Cretoxyrhina skeleton in 1894.
facts.quote: Charles R. Eastman published his analysis of the skeleton in 1894.

facts.statement: A Cretoxyrhina skeleton sold to LMU Munich was destroyed in 1944 by Allied bombing during World War II.
facts.quote: This skeleton, which Sternberg had sold to LMU Munich, was destroyed in 1944 by allied bombing during World War II.

facts.statement: George F. Sternberg discovered a second Cretoxyrhina skeleton in 1891, now housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: In 1891, Sternberg's son George F. Sternberg discovered a second O. mantelli skeleton now housed in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History as KUVP 247.

facts.statement: A Cretoxyrhina skeleton reported to be 20 feet long contained stomach contents of a Xiphactinus and about 150 visible teeth.
facts.quote: This skeleton was reported to measure 20 ft in length and consists of a partial vertebral column with skeletal remains of a Xiphactinus as stomach contents and partial jaws with about 150 teeth visible.

facts.statement: George F. Sternberg found notable Cretoxyrhina skeletons FHSM VP-323 in 1950 and FHSM VP-2187 in 1965.
facts.quote: His most notable finds were FHSM VP-323 and FHSM VP-2187, found in 1950 and 1965 respectively.

facts.statement: Collector Tim Basgall discovered a notable Cretoxyrhina skeleton in 1968 with a near-complete vertebral column and partially preserved skull.
facts.quote: In 1968, a collector named Tim Basgall discovered another notable skeleton that, similar to FHSM VP-2187, also consisted of a near-complete vertebral column and a partially preserved skull.

facts.statement: In 1958, Leonid Glickman proposed the new genus Cretoxyrhina based on the dental design of O. mantelli.
facts.quote: In 1958, Soviet paleontologist Leonid Glickman found that the dental design of O. mantelli reconstructed by Eastman made it distinct enough to warrant a new genus—Cretoxyrhina.

facts.statement: Leonid Glickman identified a second species named C. denticulata based on earlier Cretoxyrhina teeth.
facts.quote: He also identified a second species of Cretoxyrhina based on some of the earlier Cretoxyrhina teeth, which he named C. denticulata.

facts.statement: Glickman's 1964 replacement of the type species C. mantelli with 'Isurus denticulatus' is now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.
facts.quote: Originally, Glickman designated C. mantelli as the type species, but he abruptly replaced the position with another taxon identified as 'Isurus denticulatus' without explanation in a 1964 paper, a move now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.

facts.statement: Viktor Zhelezko erroneously invalidated the genus Cretoxyrhina in 2000 by synonymizing it with 'Pseudoisurus tomosus'.
facts.quote: This nevertheless led Russian paleontologist Viktor Zhelezko to erroneously invalidate the genus Cretoxyrhina in a 2000 paper by synonymizing 'Isurus denticulatus' (and thus the genus Cretoxyrhina as a whole) with another taxon identified as 'Pseudoisurus tomosus.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Mikael Siverson reinstated the genus Cretoxyrhina and moved P. vraconensis into it.
facts.quote: A 2013 study led by Western Australian Museum curator and paleontologist Mikael Siverson corrected the taxonomic error, reinstating the genus Cretoxyrhina and moving 'P'. vraconensis into it.

facts.statement: In 2010, Underwood and Cumbaa described Telodontaspis agassizensis from teeth previously identified as juvenile Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: In 2010, British and Canadian paleontologists Charlie Underwood and Stephen Cumbaa described Telodontaspis agassizensis from teeth found in Lake Agassiz in Manitoba that were previously identified as juvenile Cretoxyrhina teeth.

facts.statement: A 2013 study by Michael Newbrey reaffirmed Telodontaspis agassizensis into the genus Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: This species was reaffirmed into the genus Cretoxyrhina by a 2013 study led by American paleontologist Michael Newbrey using additional fossil material of the same species found in Western Australia.

facts.statement: Kenshu Shimada analyzed Cretoxyrhina skeletons between 1997 and 2008 using modernized techniques to research its biology.
facts.quote: Between 1997 and 2008, Japanese paleontologist Kenshu Shimada published a series of papers where he analyzed the skeletons of C. mantelli including those found by the Sternbergs using modernized techniques to extensively research the possible biology of Cretoxyrhina.

facts.statement: The name Cretoxyrhina combines 'creto' for Cretaceous and 'Oxyrhina' from Greek words meaning sharp nose.
facts.quote: Etymology Cretoxyrhina is a portmanteau of the word creto (short for Cretaceous) prefixed to the genus Oxyrhina, which is derived from the Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, "sharp") and ῥίς (rhís, "nose").

facts.statement: Although the name means 'Cretaceous sharp-nose', Cretoxyrhina is believed to have had a blunt snout.
facts.quote: When put together they mean "Cretaceous sharp-nose", although Cretoxyrhina is believed to have had a rather blunt snout.

facts.statement: The common name 'Ginsu shark' was coined in 1999 because the feeding mechanism of C. mantelli was compared to the slicing and dicing of a Ginsu knife.
facts.quote: The common name Ginsu shark, originally coined in 1999 by paleontologists Mike Everhart and Kenshu Shimada, is a reference to the Ginsu knife, as the theoretical feeding mechanisms of C. mantelli was often compared with the "slicing and dicing" when one uses the knife.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina is traditionally classified within the family Cretoxyrhinidae, which some researchers consider paraphyletic or polyphyletic.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina has been traditionally grouped within the Cretoxyrhinidae, a family of lamnoid sharks that traditionally included other genera resulting in a paraphyletic or polyphyletic family.

facts.statement: The earliest fossils of Cretoxyrhina date back to about 107 million years ago and belong to the species C. vraconensis.
facts.quote: The earliest fossils of Cretoxyrhina are dated about 107 million years old and belong to C. vraconensis.

facts.statement: The youngest known fossil of C. mantelli was found in the Bearpaw Formation of Alberta and dates to 73.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: The youngest fossil of C. mantelli was found in the Bearpaw Formation of Alberta, dating as 73.2 million years old.

facts.statement: A single tooth dated to 70.44 million years old suggests Cretoxyrhina may have survived into the Maastrichtian, though this is debated due to the brackish nature of the deposit.
facts.quote: A single tooth identified as Cretoxyrhina sp. was recovered from the nearby Horseshoe Canyon Formation and dated as 70.44 million years old, suggesting that Cretoxyrhina may have survived into the Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina teeth are distinguished by a triangular shape, razor-like non-serrated edges, visible tooth necks, and a thick enamel coating.
facts.quote: Distinguishing characteristics of Cretoxyrhina teeth include a nearly symmetrical or slanted triangular shape, razor-like and non-serrated cutting edges, visible tooth necks (bourlette), and a thick enamel coating.

facts.statement: The largest tooth discovered from Cretoxyrhina may have measured up to 8 cm in length.
facts.quote: The largest tooth discovered from this species may have measured up to 8 cm.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mantelli had a dental structure suited for "slicing and dicing" prey, using spear-like front teeth to stab and curved rear teeth to cut.
facts.quote: The structure of the tooth row shows a dental structure suited for a feeding behavior similar to modern mako sharks, having large spear-like anteriors to stab and anchor prey and curved lateroposteriors to cut it to bite-size pieces, a mechanism often informally described as "slicing and dicing" by paleontologists.

facts.statement: The elongated hyomandibula of Cretoxyrhina mantelli was believed to swing laterally, allowing for jaw protrusion and deep biting.
facts.quote: The hyomandibula is elongated and was believed to swing laterally, which would allow jaw protrusion and deep biting.

facts.statement: Most species of Cretoxyrhina are known only from fossil teeth and vertebrae because their cartilaginous skeletons fossilize poorly compared to bone.
facts.quote: Most species of Cretoxyrhina are represented only by fossil teeth and vertebra. Like all sharks, the skeleton of Cretoxyrhina was made of cartilage, which is less capable of fossilization than bone.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cretoxyrhina mantelli from the Niobrara Formation are exceptionally preserved because the chalk contains high calcium levels that promote calcification.
facts.quote: Fossils of C. mantelli from the Niobrara Formation have been found exceptionally preserved; this was due to the formation's chalk having high contents of calcium, allowing calcification to become more prevalent.

facts.statement: The largest vertebrae of Cretoxyrhina mantelli measured up to 87 mm in diameter.
facts.quote: The largest vertebra were measured up to 87 mm in diameter.

facts.statement: The best-preserved specimens of Cretoxyrhina mantelli, FHSM VP-2187 and KUVP 69102, have 218 and 201 vertebrae respectively, with only the tail tips missing.
facts.quote: Two specimens with the best-preserved vertebral columns (FHSM VP-2187 and KUVP 69102) have 218 and 201 centra, respectively, and nearly all vertebra in the column preserved; only portions of the tail tip are missing for both.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mantelli had approximately 230 vertebrae, a count unique among mackerel sharks as all living species have either fewer than 197 or more than 282.
facts.quote: Estimations of tail length calculates a total vertebral count of approximately 230 centra, which is unique as all known extant mackerel sharks possess a vertebral count of either less than 197 or greater than 282 with none in between.

facts.statement: The transition to the tail in Cretoxyrhina mantelli featured a vertebral bend of about 45 degrees, the highest angle known in living sharks and typical of fast-swimming species.
facts.quote: The transition from precaudal (the set of vertebrae before the tail vertebrae) to tail vertebrae is also marked by a vertebral bend of about 45°, which is the highest possible angle known in extant sharks and is mostly found in fast-swimming sharks, such as lamnids.

facts.statement: Features including smooth scales, a plesodic pectoral fin, and a spindle-shaped build indicate that Cretoxyrhina mantelli was capable of fast swimming.
facts.quote: These properties of the tail, along with other features such as smooth scales parallel to the body axis, a plesodic pectoral fin (a pectoral fin in which cartilage extends throughout, giving it a more secure structure that helps decrease drag), and a spindle-shaped stocky build, show that C. mantelli was capable of fast swimming.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mantelli possessed regional endothermy, likely featuring red muscles near the body axis and a rete mirabile system to conserve metabolic heat.
facts.quote: Possessing regional endothermy (also known as mesothermy), it may have possessed a build similar to modern regionally endothermic sharks like members of the thresher shark and lamnid families, where red muscles are closer to the body axis compared to ectothermic sharks (whose red muscles are closer to the body circumference), and a system of specialized blood vessels called rete mirabile (Latin for "wonderful nets") is present, allowing metabolic heat to be conserved and exchanged to vital organs.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mantelli's partially warm-blooded physiology allowed it to function efficiently in cold environments where fossils have been found.
facts.quote: This morphological build allows the shark to be partially warm-blooded, and thus efficiently function in the colder environments where Cretoxyrhina has been found.

facts.statement: It is debated whether differences in tooth size and lateral profiles among Cretoxyrhina mantelli individuals represent sexual dimorphism or individual variations.
facts.quote: In 2011, paleontologists Jim Bourdon and Mike Everhart reconstructed the dentition of multiple C. mantelli individuals based on their associated tooth sets. They discovered that two of these reconstructions show some notable differences in the size of the first intermediate (I1) tooth and lateral profiles, concluding that these differences could possibly represent sexual dimorphism or individual variations.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina had dense overlapping placoid scales with U-shaped grooves averaging 45 micrometers in width.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina possessed highly dense overlapping placoid scales parallel to the body axis and patterned in parallel kneels separated by U-shaped grooves, each groove having a mean width of about 45 micrometers.

facts.statement: The unique scale pattern of Cretoxyrhina reduced drag and enhanced speed, a trait found only in the fastest known sharks.
facts.quote: This formation of scales allows efficient drag reduction and enhanced high-speed velocity capabilities, a morphotype seen only in the fastest known sharks.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina possessed the most extreme Type 4 tail fin in mackerel sharks, with tail vertebrae curvature and cartilage angles of 49° and 133° respectively.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina also had the most extreme case of a "Type 4" tail fin, having the highest known Cobb's angle (curvature of tail vertebrae) and tail cartilage angle (49° and 133° respectively) ever recorded in mackerel sharks.

facts.statement: The Type 4 tail fin structure of Cretoxyrhina features maximum lobe symmetry for efficient fast swimming and is found only in lamnid sharks.
facts.quote: A "Type 4" tail fin structure represents a build with maximum symmetry of the tail fin lobes, which is most efficient in fast swimming; among sharks, it is only found in lamnids.

facts.statement: Although no fossil evidence exists, Cretoxyrhina is inferred to have been ovoviviparous like modern mackerel sharks.
facts.quote: Although no fossil evidence for it has been found, it is inferred that Cretoxyrhina was ovoviviparous as all modern mackerel sharks are.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Cretoxyrhina was an r-selected shark producing many infants to offset high mortality rates in waters with predators like Tylosaurus and Xiphactinus.
facts.quote: As Cretoxyrhina inhabited oligotrophic and pelagic waters where predators such as large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus and macropredatory fish like Xiphactinus were common, it is likely that it also was an r-selected shark, where many infants are produced to offset high infant mortality rates.

facts.statement: The best-preserved specimen FHSM VP-2187 was estimated to be 1.28 meters long and weigh 16.3 kg at birth, doubling its length within 3.3 years.
facts.quote: Using this linear equation, measurements were first conducted on the best-preserved C. mantelli specimen, FHSM VP-2187, by Shimada (2008). The measurements showed a length of 1.28 m and weight of about 16.3 kg at birth, and rapid growth in the first two years of life, doubling the length within 3.3 years.

facts.statement: The von Bertalanffy growth model estimated the maximum lifespan of C. mantelli to be 38.2 years, at which point it would have exceeded 7 meters in length.
facts.quote: Using the von Bertalanffy growth model on FHSM VP-2187, the maximum lifespan of C. mantelli was estimated to be 38.2 years. By that age, it would have grown over 7 m long.

facts.statement: A 2013 study proposed revising the growth ring measurements of specimen FHSM VP-2187, suggesting sexual maturity occurred at four to five years of age.
facts.quote: A remeasurement conducted by Newbrey et al. (2013) found that C. mantelli and C. agassizensis reached sexual maturity at around four to five years of age and proposed a possible revision to the measurements of the growth rings in FHSM VP-2187.

facts.statement: A 2013 study identified a syntype tooth from England that calculated a maximum length of 8 meters, making it the largest known specimen of C. mantelli.
facts.quote: The 2013 study also identified a syntype tooth of C. mantelli from England and calculated the individual's maximum length of 8 m, making the tooth the largest known specimen yet.

facts.statement: Other species like C. denticulata and C. vraconensis reached a maximum adult length of up to 4 meters.
facts.quote: Other species were estimated to have been significantly smaller. C. denticulata and C. vraconensis reached a total body length of up to 4 m as an adult.

facts.statement: C. agassizensis was estimated to reach a maximum length of 1.29 meters based on a tooth specimen measuring 12 mm in height.
facts.quote: C. agassizensis was even smaller, with an estimated total body length of up to 1.29 m based on a tooth specimen (P2989.152) measuring 12 mm tall.

facts.statement: The powerful jaws, high speed, and large size suggest Cretoxyrhina was a very aggressive predator.
facts.quote: The powerful kinetic jaws, high-speed capabilities, and large size of Cretoxyrhina suggest a very aggressive predator.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of devourment confirms Cretoxyrhina was an active apex predator feeding on diverse marine megafauna in the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhinas association with a diverse number of fossils showing signs of devourment confirms that it was an active apex predator that fed on much of the variety of marine megafauna in the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina occupied the highest trophic level, a position shared only with large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus in the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The highest trophic level it occupied was a position shared only with large mosasaurs such as Tylosaurus during the latter stages of the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina primarily hunted other active predators such as ichthyodectids, plesiosaurs, turtles, mosasaurs, and other sharks.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina mainly preyed on other active predators including ichthyodectids (a type of large fish that includes Xiphactinus), plesiosaurs, turtles, mosasaurs, and other sharks.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of Cretoxyrhina feeding includes large, deep bite marks and punctures on bones, sometimes with embedded teeth.
facts.quote: Most fossils of Cretoxyrhina feeding upon other animals consist of large and deep bite marks and punctures on bones, occasionally with teeth embedded in them.

facts.statement: A large Cretoxyrhina mantelli skeleton (KUVP 247) contained the skeletal remains of an ichthyodectid fish and a mosasaur in its stomach region.
facts.quote: There are a few skeletons of Cretoxyrhina containing stomach contents known, including a large C. mantelli skeleton (KUVP 247) which possesses skeletal remains of the large ichthyodectid Xiphactinus and a mosasaur in its stomach region.

facts.statement: A Pteranodon vertebra from the Niobrara Formation contains a Cretoxyrhina mantelli tooth lodged between the cervical vertebrae, suggesting it may have occasionally fed on pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina may have occasionally fed on pterosaurs, evidenced by a set of cervical vertebrae of a Pteranodon from the Niobrara Formation with a C. mantelli tooth lodged deep between them.

facts.statement: While uncertain if specific fossils represent predation or scavenging, pterosaurs like Pteranodon were likely natural targets for Cretoxyrhina because they routinely entered the water to feed.
facts.quote: Although it cannot be certain if the fossil itself was a result of predation or scavenging, it was likely that Pteranodon and similar pterosaurs were natural targets for predators like Cretoxyrhina, as they would routinely enter water to feed and thus be well within reach.

facts.statement: Although primarily an active hunter, Cretoxyrhina was also an opportunistic feeder that may have scavenged occasionally.
facts.quote: Although Cretoxyrhina was mainly an active hunter, it was also an opportunistic feeder and may have scavenged from time to time.

facts.statement: Many Cretoxyrhina feeding marks show no signs of healing, indicating attacks on live animals, though some marks may have resulted from scavenging.
facts.quote: Many fossils with Cretoxyrhina feeding marks show no sign of healing, an indicator of a deliberate predatory attack on a live animal, leading to the possibility that at least some of the feeding marks were made from scavenging.

facts.statement: If the feeding marks represent predation, Cretoxyrhina likely employed a hunting strategy involving a single powerful, fatal blow similar to ram feeding in modern requiem sharks and lamnids.
facts.quote: If they were indeed a result of the former, that would mean that Cretoxyrhina most likely employed hunting strategies involving a main powerful and fatal blow similar to ram feeding seen in modern requiem sharks and lamnids.

facts.statement: A 2004 study by Vittorio Gabriotti and Alessandro De Maddalena observed that modern great white sharks over 4 meters long commonly ram prey with massive force to inflict fatal blows.
facts.quote: A 2004 study by shark experts Vittorio Gabriotti and Alessandro De Maddalena observed that the modern great white shark reaching lengths of greater than 4 m commonly ram its prey with massive velocity and strength to inflict single fatal blows, sometimes so powerful that prey would be propelled out of the water by the impact's force.

facts.statement: Given its robust build, fast swimming ability, and powerful jaws reaching lengths similar to or greater than modern great white sharks, a ram-feeding hunting style was likely for Cretoxyrhina.
facts.quote: As Cretoxyrhina possessed a robust stocky build capable of fast swimming, powerful kinetic jaws like the great white shark, and reaches lengths similar to or greater than it, a hunting style like this would be likely.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina had a cosmopolitan distribution with fossils found worldwide, including North America, Europe, Israel, and Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina had a cosmopolitan distribution with fossils having been found worldwide. Notable locations include North America, Europe, Israel, and Kazakhstan.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mostly inhabited temperate and subtropical zones, with fossils found as far north as 55° N where average sea surface temperatures were estimated at 5–10°C.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina mostly occurred in temperate and subtropical zones. It has been found in latitudes as far north as 55° N, where paleoclimatic estimates calculate an average sea surface temperature of 5–10 C.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cretoxyrhina are most well known from the Western Interior Seaway, now the central United States and Canada.
facts.quote: Fossils of Cretoxyrhina are most well known in the Western Interior Seaway area, which is now the central United States and Canada.

facts.statement: In 2013, Mikael Siverson and colleagues noted that offshore Cretoxyrhina mantelli during the Turonian or early Coniacian were usually larger than those in the Western Interior Seaway, with some reaching lengths up to 8 meters, possibly 9 meters.
facts.quote: In 2013, Mikael Siverson and colleagues noted that during the Turonian or early Coniacian, Cretoxyrhina individuals living offshore were usually larger than those inhabiting the Western Interior Seaway, with some of the offshore C. mantelli fossils like one of the syntypes yielding total lengths of up to 8 m, possibly 9 m.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina mainly inhabited temperate to subtropical pelagic oceans.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina inhabited mainly temperate to subtropical pelagic oceans.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina was an extinct genus of large shark that lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 100 and 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Cretoxyrhina es un género extinto de un tiburón de gran tamaño que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, entre hace 100 a 73 millones de años.

facts.statement: The genus is occasionally known as the 'ginsu shark'.
facts.quote: Es conocido ocasionalmente como el tiburón ginsu.

facts.statement: The genus is classified within the extinct family Cretoxyrhinidae.
facts.quote: familia: Cretoxyrhinidae †

facts.statement: Evidence of interspecific interactions exists in the form of bite marks between Cretoxyrhina and large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus, which exceeded 10 meters in length.
facts.quote: Large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus, which reached in excess of 10 m in length, may have competed with Cretoxyrhina, and evidence of interspecific interactions such as bite marks from either have been found.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the extinction of Cretoxyrhina contributed to the further increase in mosasaur diversity.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the extinction of Cretoxyrhina may have helped the further increase the diversity of mosasaurs.

facts.statement: Cretoxyrhina reached its peak size during the Coniacian and gradually declined until its extinction during the Campanian.
facts.quote: Since its peak in size during the Coniacian, the size and distribution of Cretoxyrhina fossils gradually declined until its eventual demise during the Campanian.

facts.statement: Louis Agassiz first identified this shark in 1843 based on fossils found in France.
facts.quote: Este tiburón fue identificado por primera vez por el famoso naturalista suizo Louis Agassiz en 1843 a partir de fósiles hallados en Francia

facts.statement: The most complete specimen of this shark was discovered in 1890 by fossil hunter Charles H. Sternberg.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, el espécimen más completo de este tiburón fue descubierto en 1890, por el buscador de fósiles Charles H. Sternberg

facts.statement: This complete specimen includes a nearly full vertebral column found in anatomical association with nearly 250 associated teeth.
facts.quote: El espécimen comprende una columna vertebral casi completa hallada en asociación anatómica y cerca de 250 dientes asociados

facts.statement: This specimen represents an individual that was 6.1 meters long.
facts.quote: Este espécimen representa a un individuo de 6,1 metros de largo

facts.statement: The specimen was excavated from Hackberry Creek in Gove County, Kansas.
facts.quote: Fue excavado en Hackberry Creek, en el condado de Gove, Kansas

facts.statement: Paleontologists K. Shimada and M. J. Everhart named it the ginsu shark because it fed by cutting victims into pieces the size of a bite.
facts.quote: Dado que se alimentaba cortando a sus víctimas en pedazos del tamaño de una mordida, los paleontólogos K. Shimada y M. J. Everhart le dieron el nombre de tiburón ginsu

facts.statement: Fossil teeth of C. mantelli measure more than 7 centimeters long, are curved with smooth edges, and have a thick layer of enamel.
facts.quote: Los dientes fósiles de C. mantelli miden más de 7 centímetros de largo, son curvados y de bordes lisos, con una gruesa capa de esmalte

facts.statement: The ginsu shark had 34 teeth in its upper jaw and 36 in the lower jaw in each row.
facts.quote: El tiburón ginsu poseía 34 dientes en su mandíbula superior y 36 en la inferior, en cada fila

facts.statement: C. mantelli grew up to 7 meters long and rivaled the size of the modern great white shark, Carcharodon carcharias.
facts.quote: C. mantelli crecía hasta los 7 metros de largo y rivalizaba en tamaño con el actual gran tiburón blanco, Carcharodon carcharias

facts.statement: The morphology of the ginsu shark's caudal fin indicates it was an active shark capable of swimming quickly.
facts.quote: La morfología de la aleta caudal del tiburón ginsu indica que este era un tiburón activo, capaz de nadar rápidamente

facts.statement: This shark lived in world seas between the Cenomanian and Campanian stages, including the ancient Niobrara Sea of North America.
facts.quote: Este tiburón vivió en los mares del mundo entre el Cenomaniense al Campaniense, incluyendo el antiguo Mar de Niobrara de Norteamérica

facts.statement: The fossil record reveals it hunted a variety of marine animals including mosasaurs like Tylosaurus, plesiosaurs like Elasmosaurus and Xiphactinus, and protostegid turtles like Archelon.
facts.quote: El registro fósil revela que cazaba a una gran variedad de animales marinos como los mosasáuridos, como Tylosaurus, plesiosaurios como Elasmosaurus, Xiphactinus, y tortugas protostégidas como Archelon

facts.statement: Its parent group is the family Cretoxyrhinidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Cretoxyrhinidae

facts.statement: It belongs to the class Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: Class: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: Its time range extends from the Aptian to the Maastrichtian, between 121.4 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Maastrichtian (121.4 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Research by McCormack et al. (2026) using enameloid zinc isotope values provides evidence of high trophic positions for Cretoxyrhina members.
